Search for: Andaman Live Videos Home Andaman Media Delegation Visits Pasteur Institute of India in Coonoor; Experts Share Insights on Rabies Prevention for Andaman and Vaccine Research Discover more Check Voting Info Follow Politics Track Bills Andaman Media Delegation Visits Pasteur Institute of India in Coonoor; Experts Share Insights on Rabies Prevention for Andaman and Vaccine Research Sanjib Posted on 8 months ago Spread the love Sheekha Bureau Coonoor, March 13: A delegation of media representatives from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands visited the historic Pasteur Institute of India in Coonoor on 12 March as part of a study tour aimed at understanding the institute’s work in vaccine research, manufacturing and disease prevention. The visit provided the delegation with an opportunity to learn about the institute’s scientific activities and its long-standing contribution to vaccine development in the country. During the visit, officials of the institute briefed the delegation about its research programmes, vaccine manufacturing processes and the role it has played in producing vaccines for major infectious diseases. The delegation also interacted with Dr. S. Sivakumar is the Director of the Pasteur Institute of India and senior scientists, who explained how vaccines were produced in the past and how the institute plans to expand its manufacturing capabilities in the coming years. One of the key topics discussed during the interaction was rabies, a viral disease that affects all warm-blooded animals and is mainly transmitted through the saliva of infected animals, most commonly through dog bites. Experts at the institute explained that once the rabies virus enters the body, it travels through the nervous system to the brain, where it multiplies and damages neural tissue. Once the central nervous system is affected, survival chances are extremely low, making prevention and timely treatment crucial. The experts also spoke about the situation in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, where rabies has not been reported so far. They advised that strict precautions must be maintained to keep the islands rabies-free. According to them, authorities should ensure that any animals brought from the mainland, particularly dogs and cats, are properly vaccinated and accompanied by valid vaccination certificates from recognized institutions. Proper verification of such certificates is essential before allowing animals to enter the islands. The scientists also highlighted the importance of immediate first aid in the event of an animal bite. Washing the wound thoroughly with plenty of water and seeking prompt medical attention for anti-rabies treatment can significantly reduce the risk of infection. The Pasteur Institute of India, located in Coonoor in Tamil Nadu, is one of the country’s premier government institutions dedicated to vaccine research and production. Functioning as an autonomous body under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India, the institute has played a pioneering role in the development and supply of vaccines for several decades. The institute traces its origins to 1907, when it was established as the Pasteur Institute of Southern India following the death of a young woman who could not receive timely anti-rabies treatment. Over the years, it has achieved several milestones in vaccine research and manufacturing, including the production of anti-rabies vaccines, influenza vaccines and oral polio vaccines. In 2001, the institute developed a purified rabies vaccine derived from Vero cells for human use at an affordable cost, becoming the first government-controlled institution in India to do so. The move significantly helped reduce the cost of rabies vaccines in the country. Today, the institute operates modern facilities for the production of DPT group vaccines and has an installed capacity of around 130 million doses. Its laboratories are equipped with advanced technology and equipment used for large-scale vaccine production and research. The institute is also involved in academic activities, including doctoral research in microbiology, biochemistry and biotechnology. In addition, its anti-rabies treatment centre, established in 1907, continues to treat animal bite cases and collect important epidemiological data. Looking ahead, the institute plans to expand its capabilities further by establishing new biosafety level facilities for the production of viral, bacterial, conjugate and recombinant DNA vaccines. These developments are expected to strengthen India’s vaccine security and preparedness for future public health challenges. The visit provided the Andaman media delegation with valuable insights into vaccine research and public health preparedness, particularly in understanding the importance of maintaining strict preventive measures to keep regions like the Andaman and Nicobar Islands free from rabies. news.source_body_en: A media delegation from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands visited the Pasteur Institute of India in Coonoor on 12 March 2026 to learn about rabies prevention and vaccine research. The visit aimed to understand the institute’s work in developing and manufacturing vaccines for infectious diseases, including rabies. Experts highlighted that rabies, a viral disease transmitted through the saliva of infected animals, primarily via dog bites, is fatal once it reaches the central nervous system. They noted that the Andaman and Nicobar Islands have not reported any cases of rabies so far, and strict preventive measures are essential to maintain this status. The institute, established in 1907, has a long history of vaccine development and continues to treat animal bite cases and collect epidemiological data. The delegation also learned about the institute’s plans to expand its vaccine production capabilities in the future. The article does not mention any confirmed outbreak or investigation in the region, but it underscores the importance of vaccination and first aid in preventing rabies transmission.

news.content_title: Bat found in northeast St. Joseph tests positive for rabies
news.content: ST. JOSEPH, Mo. (News-Press NOW) — A bat found dead in northeast St. Joseph has tested positive for rabies after a puppy picked up the animal and carried it in its mouth, according to the St. Joseph Health Department. According to a news release, the potential exposure occurred Oct. 15, when the puppy discovered the dead bat in a residential yard. The health department submitted the bat to the Missouri State Public Health Laboratory for testing Oct. 19 and received confirmation of a positive rabies result Tuesday, Oct. 20. Health officials said there is currently no reason to believe anyone was exposed to the virus. The puppy had not been vaccinated against rabies because it was younger than the recommended vaccination age. Health department staff are working with the owners to determine appropriate observation and quarantine requirements for the pets in the household. While rabies is a serious public health concern, positive tests are relatively uncommon among animals submitted for testing in Missouri. Approximately 1% to 2% of specimens tested statewide each year are positive for rabies, with bats and skunks accounting for most positive results. The St. Joseph Health Department emphasized that the discovery does not necessarily indicate an increase in local rabies activity. Before the latest case, none of the 38 bats tested locally in 2026 had been positive. In 2025, one of 34 bats tested positive, compared with one of 25 in 2024, none of 13 in 2023 and one of 22 in 2022. The positive result comes as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has issued an advisory concerning increases in reported human exposures to rabid or potentially rabid animals in multiple U.S. jurisdictions beginning in July. Rabies is a viral disease that affects the nervous system and is nearly always fatal once symptoms develop. However, prompt medical treatment following a potential exposure can prevent infection. Health officials are reminding residents to avoid handling wild animals, even those that appear dead, and to keep pets current on rabies vaccinations. Residents should also prevent pets from roaming freely and keep them away from wildlife, noted the release. Anyone whose pet comes into contact with a bat or another potentially rabid animal should contact Animal Services and their veterinarian for guidance. Anyone who has direct contact with a bat or believes they may have been bitten or scratched should immediately contact Animal Services and a health care provider to determine whether additional precautions or treatment are needed. Residents also are encouraged to maintain their homes to prevent bats from entering attics and living spaces. Wild animals displaying unusual behavior, suspected rabies exposures or bats found inside homes should be reported to St. Joseph Animal Services at 816-271-4877. Additional information about rabies testing in Missouri is available through the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services' online rabies dashboard. news.content_original: ST. JOSEPH, Mo. (News-Press NOW) — A bat found dead in northeast St. Joseph has tested positive for rabies after a puppy picked up the animal and carried it in its mouth, according to the St. Joseph Health Department. According to a news release, the potential exposure occurred Oct. 15, when the puppy discovered the dead bat in a residential yard. The health department submitted the bat to the Missouri State Public Health Laboratory for testing Oct. 19 and received confirmation of a positive rabies result Tuesday, Oct. 20. Health officials said there is currently no reason to believe anyone was exposed to the virus. The puppy had not been vaccinated against rabies because it was younger than the recommended vaccination age. Health department staff are working with the owners to determine appropriate observation and quarantine requirements for the pets in the household. While rabies is a serious public health concern, positive tests are relatively uncommon among animals submitted for testing in Missouri. Approximately 1% to 2% of specimens tested statewide each year are positive for rabies, with bats and skunks accounting for most positive results. The St. Joseph Health Department emphasized that the discovery does not necessarily indicate an increase in local rabies activity. Before the latest case, none of the 38 bats tested locally in 2026 had been positive. In 2025, one of 34 bats tested positive, compared with one of 25 in 2024, none of 13 in 2023 and one of 22 in 2022. The positive result comes as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has issued an advisory concerning increases in reported human exposures to rabid or potentially rabid animals in multiple U.S. jurisdictions beginning in July. Rabies is a viral disease that affects the nervous system and is nearly always fatal once symptoms develop. However, prompt medical treatment following a potential exposure can prevent infection. Health officials are reminding residents to avoid handling wild animals, even those that appear dead, and to keep pets current on rabies vaccinations. Residents should also prevent pets from roaming freely and keep them away from wildlife, noted the release. Anyone whose pet comes into contact with a bat or another potentially rabid animal should contact Animal Services and their veterinarian for guidance. Anyone who has direct contact with a bat or believes they may have been bitten or scratched should immediately contact Animal Services and a health care provider to determine whether additional precautions or treatment are needed. Residents also are encouraged to maintain their homes to prevent bats from entering attics and living spaces. Wild animals displaying unusual behavior, suspected rabies exposures or bats found inside homes should be reported to St. Joseph Animal Services at 816-271-4877. Additional information about rabies testing in Missouri is available through the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services' online rabies dashboard. milk and when vaccination is necessary 450 people in Gorakhpur receive anti-rabies shots after consuming charanamrit made from suspected rabid cow’s milk; Hyderabad doctor explains whether rabies can spread through milk and when vaccination is necessary TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Oct 24, 2026, 09:07 IST Save Comments Share Aa +Text Size Small Medium Large Print Around 450 people in Gorakhpur received anti-rabies vaccinations after consuming charanamrit made with milk from a cow suspected of having rabies. A Hyderabad doctor explains why milk transmission has not been demonstrated in humans, which exposures require urgent assessment and why raw milk from a suspected rabid animal should be avoided. The news of around 450 people receiving anti-rabies vaccinations in Uttar Pradesh’s Gorakhpur district has raised an important public health question: can drinking milk from a cow suspected of having rabies expose people to the deadly infection?According to reports, people from two villages received vaccinations after consuming charanamrit, a religious offering prepared using milk from a cow that reportedly displayed unusual behaviour and died after a suspected stray dog bite. Can rabies spread through milk? Dr Sudhir Kumar, a Hyderabad-based physician, has clarified that rabies transmission through milk has not been demonstrated in humans. He also noted that consuming milk or milk products alone does not generally call for rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP).Rabies is usually transmitted when the saliva of an infected animal enters the body through a bite, scratch, broken skin or the moist lining of the eyes, nose or mouth. Drinking milk is not an established route of human rabies transmission.However, this does not make raw milk from a suspected rabid animal safe to consume. Avoid it and seek medical advice if there may have been direct contact with the animal’s saliva. Why did hundreds of people receive vaccinations? Rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms develop, making suspected exposures a serious public health concern. Health authorities may take precautionary action while investigating a possible exposure, particularly when many people are involved. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like No Monthly Payments - The New Way To Tap Home Equity - Way Easier Than HELOCComparisons.org Learn More Undo The Gorakhpur vaccination drive does not establish that the milk transmitted the virus. Nor does it confirm that the cow had rabies.A similar precautionary response followed reports of people consuming unpasteurised milk from rabid cows in Massachusetts in the 1990s. Such responses reflect caution around a potentially deadly disease, not proof of transmission through milk. When is an anti-rabies vaccine necessary? Rabies PEP may be needed after a bite or scratch from a suspected infected animal, or when its saliva directly contacts broken skin or the eyes, nose or mouth.Anyone who experiences such contact should wash the affected area thoroughly with soap and running water for 15 minutes and seek urgent medical assessment. Depending on the exposure, treatment may include rabies vaccination and rabies immunoglobulin.A person who has only consumed milk should not automatically assume vaccination is necessary. A healthcare professional must assess any additional exposure, including possible contact with saliva. Does boiling milk destroy the rabies virus? Heat can inactivate the rabies virus, and properly boiled milk is not considered an established route of rabies transmission. Nevertheless, raw milk can carry other disease-causing germs, so pasteurised or properly boiled milk is the safer choice.Avoid consuming milk from an animal suspected of having rabies, even if it appears normal. If exposure is uncertain, consult a doctor rather than relying on home treatment or assumptions about cooking. What should people remember? The key lesson from Gorakhpur is to separate precaution from confirmed transmission. The reported vaccination drive does not prove that rabies passed through the religious offering.Rabies prevention depends on recognising genuine exposure, washing wounds immediately and seeking timely medical care. Anyone worried about a possible contact should explain exactly what happened to a healthcare professional. X Register Have an account?Login here X Motoring News Health News Real Estate Cooking Gardening Advertising Digital Edition FacebookTwitterLinkedinYoutube Primary Menu Search for: Search Home Local News NSW Health Issues Urgent Bat Warning After Sharp Rise In Lyssavirus Exposure Risk EnvironmentHealth NewsLocal News NSW Health Issues Urgent Bat Warning After Sharp Rise In Lyssavirus Exposure Risk by News DeskOctober 22, 2026October 24, 20260288 Share0 NSW Health Issues Urgent Bat Warning After Sharp Rise In Lyssavirus Exposure Risk NSW Health is urging Northern Rivers residents to avoid handling bats after 43 people were assessed for bites and scratches across the state in just two weeks. NSW Health has issued an urgent warning to residents across the Northern Rivers and coastal New South Wales following a significant increase in bat bites and scratches, raising concerns about potential exposure to the deadly Australian bat lyssavirus. Between September 28 and October 10, 43 people were assessed by NSW Health after being bitten or scratched by bats, compared with just 10 during the corresponding fortnight in 2025. The incidents occurred across several regions, including Northern NSW, the Mid North Coast, Hunter New England and the Central Coast. Health authorities are particularly concerned as warmer weather increases bat activity, while natural food shortages are bringing flying-foxes into closer contact with residential communities. Deadly Virus Demands Immediate Action NSW Health Director of Health Protection Keira Glasgow warned that people should assume any bat could carry Australian bat lyssavirus, a virus closely related to rabies. “We want people to assume that any bat could carry Australian bat lyssavirus, which is a close relative to the rabies virus and very dangerous to humans,” Ms Glasgow said. Although human infections are extremely rare, the consequences can be fatal once symptoms develop. “It is incredibly rare for Australian bat lyssavirus to transmit to humans, but once symptoms of lyssavirus start in people who are scratched or bitten by an infected bat, sadly there is no effective treatment,” she said. Health authorities emphasise that prompt medical assessment and appropriate post-exposure treatment can prevent infection. What To Do If Bitten Or Scratched Anyone bitten or scratched by a bat should take immediate precautions. Wash the affected area thoroughly with soap and running water for 15 minutes. Apply an antiviral antiseptic, such as Betadine, and allow it to dry. Seek urgent medical advice about post-exposure treatment. People should not delay seeking medical assistance, even when an injury appears minor. Only appropriately trained, vaccinated and protected wildlife handlers should attempt to rescue or handle bats. Food Shortages Bringing Flying-Foxes Into Backyards NSW Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water Executive Director Conservation Programs Ingrid Emery said food shortages were contributing to unusual flying-fox behaviour. “During food shortage events, flying-foxes typically stay in feed trees during the day instead of returning to their larger colonies,” Ms Emery said. Consequently, residents may notice flying-foxes resting in backyard trees during daylight hours. Government reports indicate the shortage extends along the eastern coastline, from the Clarence Valley to the South Coast. Normal behaviour is expected to resume as natural food supplies recover, although the timing will depend on seasonal conditions. Leave Bat Rescues To Professionals Residents who discover injured, distressed or trapped bats should never attempt to handle or rescue them. Instead, contact WIRES on 1300 094 737 or a licensed local wildlife rescue organisation. NSW Health stresses that avoiding direct contact is the most effective way to prevent exposure. With flying-foxes increasingly visible throughout coastal communities, authorities are encouraging residents to remain cautious, protect children and pets from contact, and leave all bat handling to trained professionals. School Shooter: 'I Want to Apologize' Most Pet-Friendly Cities for Renters US | rabies Expert Say Risk of Rabies Could Be Rising 'We're building subdivisions into former wildlife areas' By Rob Quinn withNewser.AI Posted Oct 21, 2026 2:58 PM CDT Copied A tranquillized raccoon has its ear tagged by US Department of Agriculture wildlife specialist Robert Acabbo in Grand Isle, Vermont., Thursday, Sept. 27, 2007. (AP Photo/Toby Talbot, File) See 1 more photo Rabies might sound like a bygone threat in the US, but recent outbreaks are forcing officials to look twice. Rabid beavers in Maryland and New Jersey, infected goats at a North Carolina petting zoo, and record bat cases in California helped prompt a recent CDC advisory warning of more people needing rabies shots after risky animal encounters. But no human cases have been confirmed in 2026, and experts aren't sure whether the apparent rise is real or partly a product of heightened awareness and testing, the New York Times reports. Dr. Sara Margrey, Ohio's public health veterinarian, says more bats with rabies have been detected this year, but more bats have been sent in for testing and the percentage that test positive has not increased. "It's kind of a positive feedback loop sometimes," she says. What is clear, they say, is that rabies remains a shape-shifting danger in wildlife, from raccoons on the East Coast to skunks in the central states and foxes in Texas, where a skunk-associated variant is causing what officials call an "evolving outbreak." Unlike in many countries, where domestic dogs cause most rabies deaths in humans, bats cause the most human rabies deaths in the US, CNN reports. Officials say only a handful of Americans die from rabies every year, though some scientists say dozens more deaths might go undetected. Experts say other factors causing a possible rise in rabies risk include increased skepticism about pet vaccines, the effects of climate change on animal populations, and encroachment on animal habitats. "We're building subdivisions into former wildlife areas," Dr. Jonathan Sleeman, a wildlife veterinarian at the University of Minnesota, tells the Times. "Wildlife are increasingly adapting to human habitation, and we're encountering the wildlife more frequently." Sources tell the Times that staff cuts at the CDC have hit the agency's rabies team, which no longer advises state officials after hours. The CDC suspended rabies testing in early April due to staff shortages. Officials say the pause ended in August. Read These Next After seeing video of his son's shooting, he killed a deputy. School Shooter: 'I Want to Apologize' Most Pet-Friendly Cities for Renters US | rabies Expert Say Risk of Rabies Could Be Rising 'We're building subdivisions into former wildlife areas' By Rob Quinn withNewser.AI Posted Oct 21, 2026 2:58 PM CDT Copied A tranquillized raccoon has its ear tagged by US Department of Agriculture wildlife specialist Robert Acabbo in Grand Isle, Vermont., Thursday, Sept. 27, 2007. (AP Photo/Toby Talbot, File) See 1 more photo Rabies might sound like a bygone threat in the US, but recent outbreaks are forcing officials to look twice. Rabid beavers in Maryland and New Jersey, infected goats at a North Carolina petting zoo, and record bat cases in California helped prompt a recent CDC advisory warning of more people needing rabies shots after risky animal encounters. But no human cases have been confirmed in 2026, and experts aren't sure whether the apparent rise is real or partly a product of heightened awareness and testing, the New York Times reports. Dr. Sara Margrey, Ohio's public health veterinarian, says more bats with rabies have been detected this year, but more bats have been sent in for testing and the percentage that test positive has not increased. "It's kind of a positive feedback loop sometimes," she says. What is clear, they say, is that rabies remains a shape-shifting danger in wildlife, from raccoons on the East Coast to skunks in the central states and foxes in Texas, where a skunk-associated variant is causing what officials call an "evolving outbreak." Unlike in many countries, where domestic dogs cause most rabies deaths in humans, bats cause the most human rabies deaths in the US, CNN reports. Officials say only a handful of Americans die from rabies every year, though some scientists say dozens more deaths might go undetected. Experts say other factors causing a possible rise in rabies risk include increased skepticism about pet vaccines, the effects of climate change on animal populations, and encroachment on animal habitats. "We're building subdivisions into former wildlife areas," Dr. Jonathan Sleeman, a wildlife veterinarian at the University of Minnesota, tells the Times. "Wildlife are increasingly adapting to human habitation, and we're encountering the wildlife more frequently." Sources tell the Times that staff cuts at the CDC have hit the agency's rabies team, which no longer advises state officials after hours. The CDC suspended rabies testing in early April due to staff shortages. Officials say the pause ended in August. Read These Next After seeing video of his son's shooting, he killed a deputy. news.content_title: 2 animals test positive for rabies in Providence, Smithfield
news.content: PROVIDENCE, R.I. (WPRI) — The Rhode Island Department of Health is warning residents in Providence and Smithfield that two wild animals have tested positive for rabies. The Health Department confirmed a rabid skunk was found near Clark Road in Smithfield this week, and that a dog who came into contact with it is receiving post-rabies exposure treatment. A rabid raccoon was also discovered near Hope Street in Providence, according to the Health Department. This comes one day after the Health Department announced that a rabid skunk was found in Glocester. The Health Department has identified 43 rabid wild animals so far this year. Anyone who may have also had direct contact with the skunk or raccoon should call the Health Department’s Center for Acute Infectious Disease Epidemiology at 401-222-2577. Rabies is a potentially deadly viral disease that typically spreads through bites or scratches from an infected animal, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) . The rabies virus primarily affects the central nervous system and, if left untreated, almost always results in death. The animals most frequently infected with rabies locally are bats, skunks, raccoons and foxes, according to the Health Department. Avoid all contact with and do not feed stray or free-roaming domestic animals. Avoid all contact with and do not feed wild animals. Do not feed your animals outdoors, as this will attract other animals. This is especially dangerous when feeding large numbers of free-roaming cats. Protect your pets by always maintaining control; walk dogs on a leash or let them play in a fenced yard, and do not let pets wander unsupervised. Learn more Information bulletin Public Health Notification: Rabies Confirmed in Downtown Vancouver October 21 2026 Vancouver, B.C. – Vancouver Coastal Health (VCH) is notifying the public that a skunk captured in downtown Vancouver has tested positive for rabies. While interactions with skunks are rare, a small number of people bitten by the skunk have been assessed and received rabies vaccinations and immunoglobulin to prevent rabies. Rabies virus is found in the saliva of infected animals and can be transmitted through a bite or, less commonly, a scratch from an infected animal. Rabies virus is not transmitted through exposure to the spray, urine or feces of infected skunks. Anyone who may have been bitten or scratched, handled, picked up or otherwise had direct contact with a sick or abnormally behaving skunk in downtown Vancouver West End and Stanley Park Area (see shaded red area in map) between September 22 and October 17, 2026, should contact VCH immediately for assessment. Contact VCH Public Health at 604-675-3900 Monday-Friday (9AM-5PM). After-hours/weekends, visit an Urgent Primary Care Centre or go to an Emergency Department for assessment. Those residing outside the VCH region should contact their local health authority for assessment. About rabies Rabies is a serious viral infection that affects the brain and nervous system. It can be transmitted from an infected animal bite, scratch or direct contact with their saliva. Rabies infections in people are extremely rare in Canada. Infections are fatal but can be prevented when rabies vaccines and/or rabies immunoglobulin are administered promptly after an exposure. Bats are the only known reservoirs of rabies in B.C, meaning they can carry the disease and pass it on to other animals or people. Occasional spillovers to other animal species in specific geographical areas, including skunks, have occurred in B.C. Protect yourself from rabies Do not approach, touch, feed, capture or attempt to assist an injured or sick wild animal or unfamiliar animals. Do not touch or handle dead animals. If you observe a wild animal, including skunks, acting abnormally, please contact the BC RAPP line at 1-877-952-RAPP (7277). The animal may appear disoriented, sick or injured, or may be stumbling, active during unusual times of day, show no fear of people, or be aggressive. If you are bitten or scratched by a bat, skunk or any wild animal, wash the wound with soap and warm water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical care immediately. Protect your pets from rabies: Anyone whose dog, cat or other pet was bitten, scratched or had direct contact with a skunk in Downtown Vancouver during this identified period should contact their veterinarian promptly and advise them that their pet may have been exposed to a rabid skunk. Pet owners with no direct contact with the skunk are not at risk for rabies. To protect pets from rabies: Vaccinate all pets against rabies regularly. Supervise pets when outdoors and keep pets away from wild animals (e.g. dogs on leash). Keep pet food indoors or in a secured area to avoid attracting wild animals. If your pet is bitten or scratched by a wild animal, consult with your veterinarian immediately. To learn more about the signs and symptoms of rabies in people and animals, what to do if you or a pet is scratched or bitten by a bat or skunk, or to report wildlife-human interactions where public safety may be at risk, visit the following resources: BCCDC website - Rabies WildSafe BC - Skunks BC RAPP Line BC Wildlife Health and Alerts CONTACT: Vancouver Coastal Health media@vch.ca or 604.202.2012 (after-hours) How can we help? news.content_title: Rabies exposures on the rise in Santa Cruz County and California
news.content: An animal control officer holds a small brown bat in Illinois in 2009. The dead bat was about to be shipped to the Illinois Department of Public Health in Springfield and tested to see if it was rabid. (Stacey Wescott/Chicago Tribune/TNS) By Gabrielle Gillette | ggillette@santacruzsentinel.com | Santa Cruz Sentinel PUBLISHED: October 19, 2026 at 6:44 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 19, 2026 at 6:53 AM PDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... SANTA CRUZ — Santa Cruz County is warning of a “concerning” increase in rabies exposures and potentially rabid animals, particularly bats, in the county and across California. In 2025, the rate of bats testing positive for rabies in California increased by 37%, with 314 bats testing positive for rabies in 2025, compared to 229 in 2024, according to a media release from the Santa Cruz County Health Services Agency. Locally, Santa Cruz County has experienced an upward trend in rabid bat detection over the last three years, with nine people being exposed to rabies-positive bats as of Sept. 25 of this year, compared with only three testing positive in the complete 2025 year. Though, an increased rate of testing may have contributed to the higher number of positive bats, the release said. The agency only tests bats that have known exposure to humans, Santa Cruz County Public Health Officer Lisa Hernandez told the Sentinel. “It is important to keep pets up to date on rabies vaccination to protect both animals and people,” said Dr. Maris Brenn-White, a veterinarian at the Santa Cruz County Animal Shelter, in the media release. “Both dogs and cats should be vaccinated. Vaccinated pets provide an important second level of defense against rabies for pet owners and other people.” Though rabies is relatively rare, with fewer than 10 human rabies-related deaths reported each year in the United States, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, it poses a threat to human and animal health. Because there is no known treatment for rabies once symptoms begin, the release said, almost every person that contracts rabies will die within weeks of symptom onset. Behind bats, skunks are the second most common animal in Santa Cruz County that carry a risk of rabies, Hernandez said. Santa Cruz County recommends avoiding contact with wild animals and keeping dogs on a leash at least 150 feet away from sick or dead animals as preventative measures. If a person encounters a sick or injured wild animal, they are encouraged to call Native Animal Rescue at 831-462-0726, and to contact Mosquito & Vector Control for a home bat inspection if there is a history of finding bats indoors. Never try to remove or touch a living bat. Hernandez emphasized the importance of preventative measures, including ensuring pets are vaccinated. “Especially dogs and cats can be outdoors and and can have interactions with skunks, or if you have a cat that likes to bring you gifts, oftentimes they could be a bat,” Hernandez said. Bats that are active during the day, on the ground or unable to fly may be sick, the release said. Exposure to a bat that may have rabies can occur from saliva or tissue from the bat entering the body, such as through a bite or scratch, or through contact with a wound, mouth, nose or eyes. “Bat bites can be so small that people do not realize they have been bitten,” Hernandez said. “If you think you may have been exposed, please do not wait. Seek medical care right away. Rabies is preventable, and early action saves lives.” Bat bites may go unnoticed by a sleeping person, the release said, as they are small and can feel like a pinprick. Anyone who wakes up to find a bat in the room or finds a bat near a sleeping person, child or pet should act as though they are exposed and contact the animal shelter. After being bitten by an animal, wild or domestic, the county’s public health division said to wash the wound and seek urgent medical care to determine rabies risk and if preventative vaccines are recommended. The county also urges those who have been bitten by an animal to report the bite to the animal shelter for an assessment by the public health division. If an exposure is confirmed, domestic animals must be isolated and observed for signs of rabies, and wild animals will be tested. Animal control officers can remove a wild animal from a house. Symptoms of rabies in humans present as flu-like symptoms with fever, headache, muscle aches and fatigue, Hernandez said, as well as itching or numbness at the site of the bite. For information on rabies prevention, visit go.cdph.ca.gov/rabies . news.content_original: An animal control officer holds a small brown bat in Illinois in 2009. The dead bat was about to be shipped to the Illinois Department of Public Health in Springfield and tested to see if it was rabid. (Stacey Wescott/Chicago Tribune/TNS) By Gabrielle Gillette | ggillette@santacruzsentinel.com | Santa Cruz Sentinel PUBLISHED: October 19, 2026 at 6:44 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 19, 2026 at 6:53 AM PDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... SANTA CRUZ — Santa Cruz County is warning of a “concerning” increase in rabies exposures and potentially rabid animals, particularly bats, in the county and across California. In 2025, the rate of bats testing positive for rabies in California increased by 37%, with 314 bats testing positive for rabies in 2025, compared to 229 in 2024, according to a media release from the Santa Cruz County Health Services Agency. Locally, Santa Cruz County has experienced an upward trend in rabid bat detection over the last three years, with nine people being exposed to rabies-positive bats as of Sept. 25 of this year, compared with only three testing positive in the complete 2025 year. Though, an increased rate of testing may have contributed to the higher number of positive bats, the release said. The agency only tests bats that have known exposure to humans, Santa Cruz County Public Health Officer Lisa Hernandez told the Sentinel. “It is important to keep pets up to date on rabies vaccination to protect both animals and people,” said Dr. Maris Brenn-White, a veterinarian at the Santa Cruz County Animal Shelter, in the media release. “Both dogs and cats should be vaccinated. Vaccinated pets provide an important second level of defense against rabies for pet owners and other people.” Though rabies is relatively rare, with fewer than 10 human rabies-related deaths reported each year in the United States, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, it poses a threat to human and animal health. Because there is no known treatment for rabies once symptoms begin, the release said, almost every person that contracts rabies will die within weeks of symptom onset. Behind bats, skunks are the second most common animal in Santa Cruz County that carry a risk of rabies, Hernandez said. Santa Cruz County recommends avoiding contact with wild animals and keeping dogs on a leash at least 150 feet away from sick or dead animals as preventative measures. If a person encounters a sick or injured wild animal, they are encouraged to call Native Animal Rescue at 831-462-0726, and to contact Mosquito & Vector Control for a home bat inspection if there is a history of finding bats indoors. Never try to remove or touch a living bat. Hernandez emphasized the importance of preventative measures, including ensuring pets are vaccinated. “Especially dogs and cats can be outdoors and and can have interactions with skunks, or if you have a cat that likes to bring you gifts, oftentimes they could be a bat,” Hernandez said. Bats that are active during the day, on the ground or unable to fly may be sick, the release said. Exposure to a bat that may have rabies can occur from saliva or tissue from the bat entering the body, such as through a bite or scratch, or through contact with a wound, mouth, nose or eyes. “Bat bites can be so small that people do not realize they have been bitten,” Hernandez said. “If you think you may have been exposed, please do not wait. Seek medical care right away. Rabies is preventable, and early action saves lives.” Bat bites may go unnoticed by a sleeping person, the release said, as they are small and can feel like a pinprick. Anyone who wakes up to find a bat in the room or finds a bat near a sleeping person, child or pet should act as though they are exposed and contact the animal shelter. After being bitten by an animal, wild or domestic, the county’s public health division said to wash the wound and seek urgent medical care to determine rabies risk and if preventative vaccines are recommended. The county also urges those who have been bitten by an animal to report the bite to the animal shelter for an assessment by the public health division. If an exposure is confirmed, domestic animals must be isolated and observed for signs of rabies, and wild animals will be tested. Animal control officers can remove a wild animal from a house. Symptoms of rabies in humans present as flu-like symptoms with fever, headache, muscle aches and fatigue, Hernandez said, as well as itching or numbness at the site of the bite. For information on rabies prevention, visit go.cdph.ca.gov/rabies . School Shooter: 'I Want to Apologize' Most Pet-Friendly Cities for Renters US | rabies Expert Say Risk of Rabies Could Be Rising 'We're building subdivisions into former wildlife areas' By Rob Quinn withNewser.AI Posted Oct 21, 2026 2:58 PM CDT Copied A tranquillized raccoon has its ear tagged by US Department of Agriculture wildlife specialist Robert Acabbo in Grand Isle, Vermont., Thursday, Sept. 27, 2007. (AP Photo/Toby Talbot, File) See 1 more photo Rabies might sound like a bygone threat in the US, but recent outbreaks are forcing officials to look twice. Rabid beavers in Maryland and New Jersey, infected goats at a North Carolina petting zoo, and record bat cases in California helped prompt a recent CDC advisory warning of more people needing rabies shots after risky animal encounters. But no human cases have been confirmed in 2026, and experts aren't sure whether the apparent rise is real or partly a product of heightened awareness and testing, the New York Times reports. Dr. Sara Margrey, Ohio's public health veterinarian, says more bats with rabies have been detected this year, but more bats have been sent in for testing and the percentage that test positive has not increased. "It's kind of a positive feedback loop sometimes," she says. What is clear, they say, is that rabies remains a shape-shifting danger in wildlife, from raccoons on the East Coast to skunks in the central states and foxes in Texas, where a skunk-associated variant is causing what officials call an "evolving outbreak." Unlike in many countries, where domestic dogs cause most rabies deaths in humans, bats cause the most human rabies deaths in the US, CNN reports. Officials say only a handful of Americans die from rabies every year, though some scientists say dozens more deaths might go undetected. Experts say other factors causing a possible rise in rabies risk include increased skepticism about pet vaccines, the effects of climate change on animal populations, and encroachment on animal habitats. "We're building subdivisions into former wildlife areas," Dr. Jonathan Sleeman, a wildlife veterinarian at the University of Minnesota, tells the Times. "Wildlife are increasingly adapting to human habitation, and we're encountering the wildlife more frequently." Sources tell the Times that staff cuts at the CDC have hit the agency's rabies team, which no longer advises state officials after hours. The CDC suspended rabies testing in early April due to staff shortages. Officials say the pause ended in August. Read These Next After seeing video of his son's shooting, he killed a deputy. supplementary_news.title: 狂犬病潜伏期辟谣:多为1-3个月,不是十几年,处置越早越好(附就诊点)
supplementary_news.excerpt: 网上一直流传一种说法:狂犬病病毒能在人体里潜伏十几年甚至几十年,被咬之后可能很久以后才发病。这些年它把不少人吓得不轻;但也有另一种心态——既然潜伏期那么长,晚几天再去处理也没关系。 这两种想法其实都跑偏了。2026年9月,随着疾控部门陆续公布最新疫情数据,这个“潜伏十几年”的旧说法又被翻出来讨论。这篇文章就做一次系统的梳理:潜伏期到底多久、“十几年”的说法从哪来、为什么处置要趁早、被咬后第一步怎么 ...
